html:
The settlement of Madagascar by Austronesian sailors from Southeast Asia, who crossed the Indian Ocean some time in the first millennium CE. The date is uncertain; many scholars place it around 500, with estimates ranging a few centuries either side.

The strongest evidence is language. The Malagasy language belongs to the Austronesian family, and its closest relative is the speech of the Ma'anyan of southern Borneo, with loanwords from Malay and Javanese. Genetic studies show that the Malagasy descend from both Southeast Asian and East African ancestors.

How the voyagers came is still debated. They may have followed the coasts of India and Arabia, or sailed more directly with the monsoon winds. Austronesian traders, later of Srivijaya, roamed the Indian Ocean.

The settlers brought rice farming, outrigger canoes and other crops and customs. Bantu-speaking farmers and herders from the African mainland arrived too, bringing cattle. The two streams merged into one people. It was the westernmost reach of the Austronesian expansion, whose other branch ran east across the Pacific as far as Hawaii and Easter Island; see also the settlement of Madagascar.
